subLevels.german: Der Nil ist ein Fluss in Ägypten.

hints.hint: "Fluss" is distantly related to "flood" in English. Think something that might flood occasionally. Der Nil did once a year until the construction of the "Assuan-Staudamm"!

subLevels.reveal: "Denial" is "Verweigerung" in German, so the pun doesn't work like in English.

subLevels.german: Der Nil ist der längste Fluss der Welt (7.088 km).

hints.hint: The English translation of "längste" has the same consonants, in order.

subLevels.reveal: Why does the English sentence have "in" while the German doesn't? "der Welt" is in genitive case, so it already means "of the world".

subLevels.german: Das Nilpferd lebt im Nil, aber es ist kein Pferd.

hints.hint: Pferd = 🐴
Think of a large and dangerous "Fluss" mammal that lives "im Nil" and was worshipped "im alten Ägypten".
Nilpferd = 🦛

subLevels.reveal: Flusspferd (the more scientific term) and Nilpferd (the everyday German term) are calques — word-for-word translations of the Greek hippopotamos (river horse). English just borrowed the Greek directly. But hippos aren't horses! Their closest living relatives are whales and dolphins.

subLevels.german: WHO steht für die Weltgesundheitsorganisation.
subLevels.reveal: And now you know what people are literally saying when they wish someone "Gesundheit"!

subLevels.german: Englisch, Deutsch und Mandarin sind Weltsprachen.
subLevels.reveal: The word "Deutsch" derives from Proto-Germanic "þeudō" meaning "the people, folk". The same root gives us "Dutch", "Teuton", and the Italian word for German, "Tedesco"!

subLevels.german: Ich spreche Englisch und Deutsch, aber kein Mandarin.

hints.hint: "aber" is a conjunction.

subLevels.reveal: "Mandarin" also had a long linguistic journey, starting with the Sanskrit word "mantrin" meaning a minister, via Malay "menteri", and then to Portuguese "mandarim". The Portuguese used this word for the scholar-officials of the Qing court, and for the court's lingua franca.

subLevels.german: Spanisch spreche ich mit Gott, Italienisch mit Frauen, Französisch mit Männern und Deutsch mit meinem Pferd.
subLevels.attribution: Karl V, Kaiser des Heiligen Römischen Reiches

hints.hint: The word order of the first clause may be a bit confusing, but you know or can easily guess most of the words. Translate into natural English word order.
"Frauen" and "Männern" are plural and contrast in gender, and the latter is pretty close to its English equivalent!

subLevels.reveal: Were you able to decode Karl V's title? "Kaiser" was borrowed from Latin "Caesar", as was Russian "Tsar/Czar". And "Reich" ("empire", "realm") still appears in English as the "-ric" in "bishopric".

subLevels.german: Zweiter Weltkrieg
subLevels.instruction: Sort the countries into the correct group (−1 pt per wrong placement)
subLevels.reveal: You've probably worked out what "Zweiter" means. The "First" would have been "Erster" — can you think of an English word containing the now-rare morpheme "erst"?

subLevels.german: „Krieg und Frieden“ ist ein russisches Buch von Leo Tolstoi.

hints.hint: This is notorious as a very "langes Buch".

subLevels.reveal: The word I was thinking of with "erst" ("first", "former" in German) is "erstwhile"!

subLevels.german: Friede den Hütten, Krieg den Palästen!
subLevels.attribution: Georg Büchner, Deutscher Dramatiker und Revolutionär

hints.hint: "Hütten" and "Palästen" are two contrasting types of abodes, both close to their English equivalents.

subLevels.reveal: And on that stirring call to action, congratulations on finishing Level 3!
